claims.text: A controlled sub-nanometer PtOx surface layer forms on nanoscale platinum catalysts following electrochemical potential cycling.
The PtOx surface layer modulates the catalyst's d-band electronic structure.
PtOx-induced electronic modulation optimizes or weakens the binding of key oxygenated reaction intermediates.
The altered intermediate binding promotes complete 12-electron oxidation of ethanol to CO2.
The PtOx layer reduces poisoning by CO-like species.
The PtOx layer acts as a protective barrier that limits catalyst degradation during prolonged potential cycling.
The relevant initial catalyst may be either nanoscale platinum or a carbon-supported PtRu alloy with a fully reduced surface.
Potential cycling can prepare a reproducible, thin PtOx surface state distinct from a fully reduced baseline.
An ordered PtOx surface layer can form dynamically and remain stable during ethanol oxidation.
Relative to the fully reduced catalyst, the pre-oxidized catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential.
Relative to the fully reduced catalyst, the pre-oxidized catalyst will show greater CO2 selectivity and less acetaldehyde or other partial-oxidation products.
Relative to the fully reduced catalyst, the pre-oxidized catalyst will retain performance better during extended potential cycling.
The proposed beneficial PtOx state is expected to exist and operate between 0.6 and 1.2 V versus RHE in 0.5 M H2SO4 containing 1 M ethanol at 25 degrees Celsius.
At potentials causing complete oxidation or reduction, the controlled PtOx state will not be maintained and its beneficial effects may disappear.
